verdicts.why: Names the continuum itself; no attitude toward anything, and the sentences use it as a bare measure.
A clock reading is a plain fact; nothing is approved or dismissed by calling it the time.
An occasion's experience is neutral in itself; any judgement comes from the modifier (good time, hard time), not from the noun.
Musical time is a technical term for rhythmic division; it describes without judging.
Imprisonment is a bad referent, but 'time' names the span flatly and takes no side on the prisoner.
The physics coordinate is purely descriptive; there is nothing here to judge.
Daylight hours are a plain fact of the calendar; no attitude is carried.
One's waking or working hours are named without approval or contempt.
A day assigned to a purpose (wedding day, market day) is neutral labelling, not evaluation.
'His day' names a period of flourishing without judging it; any wistfulness in 'had his day' comes from the past tense, not the noun.
A planet's rotation period is a technical measure with no attitude attached.
The sidereal day is astronomical bookkeeping; nothing to approve or dismiss.
The authority is part of the meaning (tell vs ask), not an attitude the speaker adds toward the person told.
'I can tell' names discernment plainly; it judges neither the discerner nor the thing discerned.
Telling things apart is neutral distinguishing; no evaluation rides on the verb.
Informing with confidence is the verb's meaning; it does not colour the hearer or the news.
Crediting someone's word is a plain mental act; unlike 'swallow' or 'fall for', it does not mock the believer.
Having a faith is stated without approval or scorn; the word takes no side on religion.
An intuitive sense of something is named neutrally; 'hunch' might be casual, but 'feeling' is plain.
The atmosphere of a place can be good or bad, but the noun itself does not say which.
Tactile sensation is a physiological fact; no attitude is carried.
A woman in the armed forces is named plainly; the word passes no verdict on her.
Constituting an addition is a plain relation; nothing is being praised or dismissed.
Bestowing a quality (adds charm, adds cost) is neutral; the judgement, if any, sits in the object, not the verb.
Arithmetic summing is as plain as a word can be.
Considering something due states the speaker's stance as meaning; it does not colour the person or thing expected.
Awaiting a birth is described without any attitude beyond the meaning.
'Expecting' for pregnancy is a mild conventional euphemism but carries no approval or disapproval of the pregnancy.
'Of moment' means important; that is its meaning, and the formal register is not an attitude toward the thing.
The physics term for a turning force is purely technical.
